precepts.text: Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman, and the Lord heard it.
precepts.point: The Lord said, if her father had but spit in her face, should she not be ashamed seven days? Let her be shut out from the camp seven days, and after that let her be received in again. That is the same law working here: the leper is put without the camp.

note.label: Leviticus 13: The Law of the Plague of Leprosy

precepts.why:
Miriam is the example of the leper put without the camp. “Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married.” They said, “Hath the Lord indeed spoken only by Moses? hath he not spoken also by us?”

Miriam was trying to usurp authority over the man. “And the Lord heard it.” What followed shows the law of Leviticus 13 in motion.

precepts.text: The cloud departed from off the tabernacle, and Miriam became leprous, white as snow.
precepts.point: The Lord said, if her father had but spit in her face, should she not be ashamed seven days? Let her be shut out from the camp seven days, and after that let her be received in again. That is the same law working here: the leper is put without the camp.

note.label: Leviticus 13: The Law of the Plague of Leprosy

precepts.why:
The Lord heard Miriam speak against Moses, and the judgment came: “the cloud departed from off the tabernacle; and, behold, Miriam became leprous, white as snow: and Aaron looked upon Miriam, and, behold, she was leprous.”

Here is a leper “in whom the plague is”, the very case Leviticus 13:45-46 speaks of, and it came upon her for speaking against Moses.

precepts.text: Let her be shut out from the camp seven days, and after that received in again; the leper dwells without the camp.
precepts.point: The Lord said, if her father had but spit in her face, should she not be ashamed seven days? Let her be shut out from the camp seven days, and after that let her be received in again. That is the same law working here: the leper is put without the camp.

note.label: Leviticus 13: The Law of the Plague of Leprosy

precepts.why:
“the leper in whom the plague is” is defiled all the days the plague is in him: “he shall dwell alone; without the camp shall his habitation be.” That is exactly what happened to Miriam.

“And the Lord said unto Moses, If her father had but spit in her face, should she not be ashamed seven days? let her be shut out from the camp seven days, and after that let her be received in again. And Miriam was shut out from the camp seven days: and the people journeyed not till Miriam was brought in again.”

That is the same law working here: the leper is put without the camp, and only when she was clean was she received in again.

points: The plague of leprosy is discerned by the priest. When the hair in the plague is turned white and the plague in sight is deeper than the skin of the flesh, it is a plague of leprosy and the priest pronounces him unclean; if not, the priest shuts him up seven days, and seven days more if the plague is at a stay, and if the plague is somewhat dark and spread not, it is but a scab and he is pronounced clean; but a scab that spreads much abroad after his cleansing is a leprosy.

note.label: Leviticus 13: The Law of the Plague of Leprosy

points: If the leprosy break out abroad and cover all the flesh from head to foot, and it be all turned white, the priest shall pronounce him clean.

That is the albino: if the leprosy covers all the skin, as in an albino, he is still clean. A man can be albino and still be Israel; if his father is Judah, he is clean. It is not about your skin, it is about your nationality.

note.label: Leviticus 13: The Law of the Plague of Leprosy

points: For a plague upon the head or the beard, if it be in sight deeper than the skin, and there be in it a yellow thin hair, it is a dry scall, even a leprosy upon the head or beard, and the priest pronounces him unclean.

Yellow thin hair is called a plague. Our hair does not come like that; the nations that have blonde hair are naturally that way. When Israel, blacks, Hispanics, and Native Americans dye their hair blonde, they are taking after the customs of Esau, emulating who they want to be like, and the word calls that yellow thin hair a plague on our people.
There is no law against color as such: the scripture names yellow thin hair; but go with what the word says.

note.label: Leviticus 13: The Law of the Plague of Leprosy

points: So do not assume against a brother: if he goes bald naturally, the word says the man is clean, and a brother may be forehead bald with hair further back you cannot see.

note.label: Leviticus 13: The Law of the Plague of Leprosy

points: The man whose hair is fallen off his head is bald, yet is he clean; and he whose hair is fallen off toward his face is forehead bald, yet is he clean.

note.label: Leviticus 13: The Law of the Plague of Leprosy

points: The leper in whom the plague is, his clothes shall be rent, his head bare, a covering upon his upper lip, and he shall cry, Unclean, unclean; all the days the plague is in him he is defiled, and he shall dwell alone, without the camp.

note.label: Leviticus 13: The Law of the Plague of Leprosy

points: The Lord said, if her father had but spit in her face, should she not be ashamed seven days? Let her be shut out from the camp seven days, and after that let her be received in again. That is the same law working here: the leper is put without the camp.

note.label: Leviticus 13: The Law of the Plague of Leprosy

points: The plague of leprosy can be in a garment, woollen or linen, in the warp or woof or in any thing made of skin, greenish or reddish; it is shewed unto the priest and shut up seven days, and if the plague be spread in the garment it is a fretting leprosy: the garment is burnt in the fire. As with Miriam, the clothing wherein the plague is had to be dealt with.

note.label: Leviticus 13: The Law of the Plague of Leprosy

points: If the plague be not spread, the thing is washed and shut up seven days more; if the plague have not changed his colour it is burnt, and if it be somewhat dark after washing, the piece is rent out; if it appear still, it is a spreading plague and burnt with fire; and the garment that the plague departs from is washed the second time and shall be clean. This is the law of the plague of leprosy in a garment, to pronounce it clean or to pronounce it unclean.
